prompt: Nora tells her enrolled agent, Luis, that she had no cryptocurrency activity in 2025. Luis already has Nora's own exchange statement, and it shows sales during the year. Luis is deciding whether he may rely on her denial and leave those sales off the return. What should he do?

options.text: Rely on the denial, because a practitioner may ignore a document already in the file when the client says the opposite.
Leave the sales off, because an exchange statement is not tax information a preparer has to reconcile.
Do not rely on the denial; the statement he already has makes that reliance unreasonable.
Report Nora to IRS Criminal Investigation before he asks her about the statement in his file.

explanation: Circular 230 allows good-faith reliance on what a client says only when that reliance is reasonable. A practitioner may not ignore information actually known to the practitioner. Luis already holds Nora's exchange statement showing sales, so treating her denial as complete is not reasonable reliance. He has to reconcile the statement before he signs.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an exchange statement with a document outside the return. Sales on the client's own statement are facts the preparer cannot set aside.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a duty to inquire with a criminal referral. The next step is to resolve the inconsistency with the client, not to report her before asking.

prompt: Priya prepares a 2025 Form 1040 and claims a deduction that lacks substantial authority. She does not disclose the position on the return. The position understates the client's liability. Which preparer penalty fits that undisclosed position?

options.text: No preparer penalty applies, because substantial authority is tested only after an examination opens.
Only the taxpayer's accuracy-related penalty can apply; the preparer has no penalty of her own for the position.
The higher willful-or-reckless preparer penalty applies whenever a position is left undisclosed.
The ordinary unreasonable-position preparer penalty applies to the undisclosed position.

explanation: Section 6694(a) is the preparer penalty for an understatement caused by an unreasonable position. An undisclosed position needs substantial authority. The stem does not give her fee, so the penalty is not computed as a dollar amount.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the taxpayer's accuracy-related penalty with the preparer's penalty. Section 6694 is a separate penalty on the preparer for an unreasonable position.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses nondisclosure with willful or reckless conduct. Leaving a weak position undisclosed supports the ordinary penalty; it does not by itself impose the higher one.

The person who prepared the return for pay must have their own PTIN and sign that return.
The signature is fine if the client agreed in the engagement letter that the firm may pick any name.

distractorExplanations.d: Confuses client consent with the signing rule. A client cannot authorize someone else's name in place of the person who prepared the return for pay.

prompt: A client texts from work and asks her enrolled agent to email her full Social Security number so she can finish a lender's form. The firm's ordinary email is not encrypted. What is the sound practice for sending that number?

Send the full Social Security number through a secure channel, not in ordinary email.
Email the full number with the word confidential in the subject line, because that legend is the safeguard.
Text the full number to the client's work phone, because a text is outside the precaution that applies to email.

explanation: A preparer has to protect a taxpayer identification number. Putting the full Social Security number in ordinary unencrypted email exposes it. prompt: An enrolled agent maps the current three-year cycle as 72 hours of federal tax classes and then 6 more hours of ethics on top of that 72. How do the ethics hours count toward the cycle requirement?

They count only if the enrolled agent sits the Special Enrollment Examination again during the same cycle.

prompt: A CPA tells an enrolled agent that Circular 230 is only an enrolled-agent handbook, so a CPA or an attorney who practices before the IRS may ignore it. The CPA and the attorney both represent clients in examinations. Who must follow Circular 230?

The enrolled agent, the CPA, and the attorney all follow it when practicing before the IRS.
Only the attorney, because Circular 230 is a court rule for lawyers rather than a Treasury practice rule.
No practitioner who holds a current PTIN, because renewing the PTIN takes the place of Circular 230.

prompt: An enrolled agent tells a new client that the fee for preparing the original 2025 Form 1040 will be whatever the refund turns out to be. The refund is not known when they agree. Which statement describes that fee under Circular 230?

options.text: It is allowed unless the refund is large, because a contingent fee is tested against the size of the refund.
It is the preferred way to price an original return, because the client pays only when a refund is issued.
It is a barred contingent fee on an original return; an unconscionable fee is also barred.
It is allowed once the client signs Form 8879, because the e-file authorization approves the fee.

explanation: Circular 230 bars an unconscionable fee for a matter before the IRS. A fee set at whatever the refund is, for preparing an original return, is also a contingent fee, and a contingent fee for an original return is generally barred. Form 8879 authorizes an e-file signature. It does not approve the fee.

distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Form 8879 with a fee agreement. The e-file signature authorization does not make a contingent fee on an original return acceptable.
